description:
Wesam Saad continues the obedience chapter by restating salvation through grace and faith in Christ. Obedience is a direction for growth, not a way to earn acceptance. Returning to the question about persecution, he examines 1 Peter 2:20–23. The distinction is between suffering as a consequence of wrongdoing and patiently enduring suffering for doing what is right. Christ supplies the example: He neither retaliated with abuse nor threatened those who hurt Him, but entrusted Himself to the righteous Judge. Wesam connects that trust with God seeing faithful endurance and rewarding it. Hebrews 12:2 adds the example of Jesus enduring the cross with joy set before Him.

Romans 12:1 then describes the believer’s body as a living, holy sacrifice. Wesam applies that whole-life dedication to reactions, relationships and private choices, rather than limiting worship to a church gathering. The discussion of future reward draws on 1 Peter’s promised inheritance and the appearing of the chief Shepherd. Finally, 1 John 2 and Matthew 7 distinguish genuine obedience from a merely verbal profession or impressive religious activity. He presents obedience as evidence of knowing Christ, while maintaining the opening distinction between grace and earning salvation. Listeners are urged to examine whether Christ’s lordship is visible at home and outside public ministry.

questions.question: What distinction does Wesam draw between the two kinds of suffering in 1 Peter 2?
questions.answer: He contrasts enduring consequences after wrongdoing with doing what is right, suffering for it and enduring patiently. The outward suffering and patience may look similar, but the starting action differs. He reads the passage as commending patient endurance when obedience itself attracts mistreatment.

questions.question: What pattern does he understand believers to be called to follow?
questions.answer: Wesam describes the pattern as doing good, suffering for it and enduring with patience. He connects the words called for this purpose with Christ’s example, rather than treating suffering as an isolated event without obedience or endurance. He presents this as part of life in a world opposed to God.

questions.question: How does Christ’s response to unjust suffering shape that pattern?
questions.answer: Wesam points to Christ committing no sin, not retaliating when reviled and not threatening others while suffering. Christ entrusted Himself to the one who judges righteously. The example therefore concerns both continuing to do right and refusing a retaliatory response.

questions.question: Why does Wesam stress God’s righteous judgement as a motive for endurance?
questions.answer: He argues that God sees obedience and patient suffering and will not let it go to waste. His emphasis includes future reward for faithfulness, rather than only punishment of wrongdoers. He connects this with the joy set before Christ in Hebrews 12:2.

questions.question: Does the favour discussed mean only that God is presently pleased?
questions.answer: Wesam affirms that God is pleased, but also points to future reward in 1 Peter. He cites the imperishable inheritance, praise and honour at Christ’s revelation, and the unfading crown promised when the chief Shepherd appears. He therefore encourages hopeful endurance without promising immediate earthly relief.

questions.question: What does presenting the body as a living, holy sacrifice mean in his explanation?
questions.answer: From Romans 12:1, Wesam describes a whole person set apart for God in continuing daily life. He applies it to resisting angry retaliation and considering relationships and what one watches. Worship is therefore not confined to a meeting; bodily choices are part of the commitment to obey God.

questions.question: How does he relate obedience to knowing Christ without making it the price of salvation?
questions.answer: Wesam begins with salvation by grace through faith in Christ and later says obedience shows whether a profession is genuine. From 1 John, he argues that keeping Christ’s commandments is evidence of knowing Him. The distinction is between obedience as a sign of salvation and obedience as a means of earning it.

questions.question: Why are impressive words or religious activities insufficient in the Matthew 7 discussion?
questions.answer: Wesam contrasts saying Lord, Lord and citing spectacular works with doing the Father’s will. He understands Christ’s rejection as the absence of a genuine relationship, rather than a lack of knowledge about the person. Public claims therefore cannot substitute for a life that actually follows Christ’s commands.

questions.question: What practical self-examination does Wesam call for at the end?
questions.answer: He asks whether Christ is treated as Lord at home, in spare time and in private choices, including what a person watches. He also applies that examination to himself, saying public ministry should not be the only basis for judging his life. The call is for obedience beyond the church doors, rather than a convincing public profession alone.
